title: Chromatography
examples: How do I know if the spot is pure?
What does a high Rf value mean?
Can chromatography separate things in the air?

explain.say: Today we are looking at chromatography for separation.
First we look at the solvent front moving up the paper.
Next we find the spot we are measuring for its Rf value.
The Rf value tells us how far a substance traveled.
If we see only one spot, the substance is likely pure.
In real life, chromatography separates ink colours in a marker.

faq.q: What does Rf stand for in this process?
faq.a: Rf stands for the retention factor. It is a number used to identify a substance.

faq.q: If my Rf value is zero, what does that mean?
faq.a: An Rf value of zero means the substance did not move at all. It stayed right where you put it.
asks: Can a spot have an Rf of zero?
What if the spot doesn't move?

faq.q: Does the solvent front move at the same speed always?
faq.a: The solvent front moves at a relatively steady rate during the process. This consistency is important for accurate measurements.

faq.q: How do I know if a mixture has more than two things?
faq.a: You must see three or more distinct, separated spots on the paper. Each spot represents a different substance.
asks: How many spots mean how many things?
Can I tell if there are three things?

faq.q: Is the paper type important for chromatography?
faq.a: Yes, the stationary phase, which is the paper, affects how well the separation happens. Different papers work better for different substances.
asks: What kind of paper should I use?

facts: Chromatography separates mixtures into individual components.
The Rf value is calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the spot by the distance travelled by the solvent front.
A pure substance will show only one spot on the chromatogram.
The solvent front marks the maximum distance the solvent traveled up the paper.

quiz.say: If a spot travels 4 centimetres and the solvent front travels 10 centimetres, what is the Rf value?
quiz.why: The Rf value is the ratio of the spot distance to the front distance, so four divided by ten equals zero point four.

wrong.0: You cannot add the two distances together. Rf is a ratio, not a total length.
wrong.1: You must divide the spot distance by the front distance, not the other way around.
wrong.2: Subtraction is used for finding differences, but Rf requires division.

quiz.say: What does it mean if you see three distinct coloured spots?
quiz.why: Seeing multiple spots means the original sample was a mixture of at least three different substances.

wrong.0: The solvent moving up is normal; the spots show what was in the sample.
wrong.1: The spots are evidence of the sample, not dirt on the paper itself.
wrong.3: Pure substances only produce one spot, so this answer is incorrect.

quiz.say: If a substance has a very low Rf value, where did it travel?

options.show: It did not move at all.
options.say: It did not move at all.

options.show: It travelled faster than the front.
options.say: It travelled faster than the front.

quiz.why: A low Rf value means the substance moved slowly, suggesting it stuck strongly to the paper.

wrong.0: If it travelled the full length, the Rf value would be close to one.
wrong.1: This would mean an Rf value of zero, which is only one possibility.
wrong.2: Nothing can travel faster than the solvent front in this setup.
